question.text: What is the relation between the length of the chord and its distance from the center of the circle?

answers.answer: The closer a chord is to the center, the longer it is, and the farther it is from the center, the shorter it is.
solution: Look at the chords from A in the figure and their distances from M.
The rule says: the closer the chord is from the center, the longer its length is, and vice versa.

checks.resolve_answer: The closer a chord is to the center, the longer it is, and vice versa (longer chord ⇔ smaller distance from the center).

question.text: If the chords are equal in length, what can you conclude?

answers.answer: Equal chords in a circle are equidistant from the center.
solution: Take chords of equal length in the same circle.
By the theorem, chords of equal length are equidistant from the center.
The same holds in congruent circles.

checks.resolve_answer: Equal chords in a circle (or in congruent circles) are equidistant from the center.

question.text: If the chords are equidistant from the center of the circle, what do we expect?

answers.answer: We expect the chords to be equal in length.
solution: Take chords at equal distances from the center.
By the converse of the theorem, chords equidistant from the center(s) are equal in length.

checks.resolve_answer: We expect the chords to be equal in length (converse of the theorem).

solution: Read the lengths: AB = 8 cm and CD = 8 cm.

question.text: In the figure opposite MF < ME, Complete: ∵ MF < ME ∴ X + 1 > ......... ; ∵ CD is a chord in circle M ∴ X ≤ ......... i.e: X ∈ ......... ; ∴ CD > ......... X > ......... ∴ CD ≤ ......... Thus ......... < X ≤ .........
question.notes: Question number 2 printed in a circle; the first line is the stem. Blanks as printed.

solution: Read the figure: CD = X+1, AB = 7 cm, radius = 5 cm so diameter = 10 cm.
MF < ME, so CD is closer to the center than AB, so CD is longer: X+1 > 7, i.e. CD > 7.
X+1 > 7 gives X > 6.
CD is a chord, so it is at most the diameter: CD ≤ 10, i.e. X+1 ≤ 10, so X ≤ 9.
Thus 6 < X ≤ 9.

question.text: Study the figure then complete:

answers.answer: MX = MY; ME = MO; EX = OY
solution: AB = CD, so the chords are equidistant from the center: MX = MY.
ME and MO are radii of the circle, so ME = MO.
Subtract: ME − MX = MO − MY.
So EX = OY.

checks.resolve_answer: MX = MY; ME = MO; EX = OY

question.text: Study the figure then complete:
question.stem: If: $AB = CD$, then: $MX = \ldots$; in $\triangle MXY$: since $m(\angle XMY) = 100^\circ$, therefore $m(\angle MXY) = \ldots^\circ$

solution: AB = CD, so MX = MY.
In triangle MXY, MX = MY, so the base angles are equal: m(∠MXY) = m(∠MYX).
The angles sum to 180°, so 2·m(∠MXY) = 180° − 100° = 80°.

question.text: Study the figure then complete:
question.stem: If: M and N are two congruent circles, $AB = CD$, then: $MX = \ldots$ and the figure MXYN $\ldots$

answers.answer: MX = NY; MXYN is a parallelogram (a rectangle)
solution: The circles are congruent and AB = CD, so the chords are equidistant from the centers: MX = NY.
MX ⊥ DA and NY ⊥ DA, so MX ∥ NY.
Two opposite sides MX and NY are equal and parallel.
So MXYN is a parallelogram (with right angles, a rectangle).

checks.resolve_answer: MX = NY; the figure MXYN is a rectangle

question.text: In the figure opposite: Triangle ABC is inscribed in circle M, in which $m(\angle B)=m(\angle C)$, X is the midpoint of $\overline{AB}$, $\overline{MY}\perp\overline{AC}$. Prove that: $MX=MY$

answers.answer: Since ∠B = ∠C, AB = AC, and equal chords are equidistant from the center, so MX = MY.
solution: Given: m(∠B) = m(∠C), X is the midpoint of AB, MY ⊥ AC.
In triangle ABC, m(∠B) = m(∠C), so AB = AC.
X is the midpoint of AB, so MX ⊥ AB.
In circle M, AB = AC with MX ⊥ AB and MY ⊥ AC.
So MX = MY (theorem). Q.E.D.

checks.resolve_answer: Since m(∠B) = m(∠C), the sides opposite are equal: AC = AB. X is the midpoint of AB so MX ⟂ AB, and MY ⟂ AC. In the same circle, equal chords AB = AC are equidistant from the center, therefore MX = MY. (Q.E.D.)

question.text: If M and N are two congruent circles and intersecting at A and B. Is $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ an axis to $\overline{MN}$? Explain your answer.

answers.answer: Yes, AB is the axis of symmetry of MN, because AB is the perpendicular bisector of MN.
solution: A and B are on both circles, which have equal radii r, so MA = NA = r and MB = NB = r.
A is equidistant from M and N, and so is B.
So the line AB is the perpendicular bisector of MN.
So AB is an axis of symmetry of MN.

checks.resolve_answer: Yes. Both circles are congruent, so MA = MB = NA = NB, so M and N each lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, which means line MN is perpendicular to AB at its midpoint. Equivalently, AMBN is a rhombus whose diagonals bisect each other perpendicularly, so line AB is the axis of symmetry (perpendicular bisector) of MN.
